implementation_notes: Rack is the Ruby realization: a middleware is an object that stores the downstream app in initialize(app, *args) and implements call(env), which invokes app.call(env) and post-processes the [status, headers, body] triple; Rack::Builder (or Rails' config.middleware) is the FilterManager and the ordered stack is the FilterChain. It applies to every request the server handles, including ones no controller sees. Use it for transport concerns; use controller filters when the concern needs controller context.
code_sketch:
class Timing
  def initialize(app)
    @app = app                                  # downstream chain, once at boot
  end
  def call(env)
    t0 = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)     # pre
    status, headers, body = @app.call(env)                   # next middleware or app
    headers['x-runtime'] = (Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC) - t0).round(4).to_s
    [status, headers, body]                                  # post
  end
end
# config.ru: use Timing; run App
pitfalls: The response body is a separate Rack body object: consuming it to post-process forces buffering and breaks streaming unless a wrapped body passes chunks through and calls close.
Middleware are instantiated once at boot and shared across threads, so instance variables are cross-request state.
Rack 3 requires lowercase header keys; a middleware that writes 'X-Runtime' instead of 'x-runtime' violates the spec and Rack::Lint will catch it.

variants.name: Rails controller filters (before_action/around_action)
variants.implementation_notes: Rails layers a controller-scoped chain on top of Rack: before_action runs before an action and halts the chain when it renders or redirects, around_action wraps the action so code after yield is the post-processing step, and the callbacks are inherited and can be skipped per controller. This is the convenient level for concerns that need controller context (params, current_user, templates), and the wrong level for guarantees that must hold for every request - a skipped callback or a route outside the controller leaves the request unguarded.
variants.code_sketch:
class ApplicationController < ActionController::Base
  before_action :require_login
  around_action :timed

  def timed
    t0 = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)      # pre
    result = yield                                            # the action
    response.set_header('x-runtime',
      (Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC) - t0).round(4).to_s)   # post
    result
  end
end
pitfalls: Callbacks are per controller class: skip_before_action or a route handled outside the controller silently removes the filter, so authentication that must be total belongs in Rack middleware.
Rendering or redirecting inside a before_action halts the chain, but an around_action still executes its post-yield code around that halted response.
An exception raised after yield inside an around_action turns a successful action into a 500 unless it is caught.
